segments.text: <curious>Let's start with the big idea.</curious> A determinant takes a whole square grid of numbers and hands you back just one number.
That single number is not random. It captures the essence of the grid, especially whether the rows point in genuinely independent directions.
You already know its smallest version. For a two by two grid the determinant is the cross-difference: a d minus b c.
Geometrically, this value is the signed area of the parallelogram drawn by the two rows treated as arrows.
Step up to a three by three grid and the determinant becomes the signed volume of the box built from its three rows.
Here is the punchline: if that volume is zero, the rows have secretly collapsed onto each other and carry no new information.

An analogy: just as net run rate squeezes a whole cricket season into one number that says something real about a team, a determinant squeezes a whole square table into one number, telling you whether the related system has a clean unique answer.
The value is written three ways: d e t A, vertical bars around A, or the Greek letter delta. Learn to read all three.
The bar notation came from Arthur Cayley in eighteen forty one, growing out of Cramer's seventeen fifty work on equations. An order n determinant hides n factorial terms.
Before we compute anything, two non-negotiable rules decide when a determinant even makes sense.
Rule one: a determinant exists only for a square matrix. A two by three arrangement has no determinant at all.
The order one determinant is simply the entry itself. The single bar here means determinant, not modulus.
So the determinant of minus five is minus five, even though its absolute value is five. This trips up almost everyone once.
Rule two: the Sarrus diagonal shortcut we will meet works for three by three grids only. Never stretch it to two by two or four by four.
The reason is structural. The expansion pairs each row with a matching column, and only a square keeps that pairing balanced.
One more framing: a determinant is a scalar, a pure dimensionless number. It carries no units, no matter what the entries mean.
With these guardrails in place, we can safely build the actual expansion machinery next.
Cofactor expansion has a reliable four-step rhythm. Follow it and you rarely make sign errors.
Step one, before writing anything, scan for the row or column with the most zeros. Every zero entry deletes a whole two by two evaluation.
Step two, walk along that chosen line. For each entry, multiply it by the two by two determinant left after deleting its row and column, its minor.
Step three, attach the checkerboard sign, minus one to the i plus j, to each term.
Step four, add the signed terms together. That sum is your determinant.
Why do the signs alternate? They encode the orientation flip that happens each time you skip over a row and a column.
Sarrus is faster on a dense grid but purely mechanical. It offers no zero-skipping, so on a sparse grid, row expansion wins.
When a determinant with an unknown x is set equal to a value, expand it fully into a polynomial in x, then solve. Simplify first whenever you can.
Let's evaluate one two by two and one three by three, carefully watching every sign.
First the two by two. Cross-difference: three times four, minus, minus two times five.
That is twelve plus ten, which gives twenty two. The double negative quietly flipped into a plus, watch that.
Now the three by three. We will expand along the first row, keeping the plus, minus, plus signs.
Each entry pairs with its minor: two times its minor, minus one times its minor, plus three times its minor.
The minors evaluate to: four minus two is two; zero minus five is minus five; zero minus twenty is minus twenty.
Putting it together: two times two, minus one times minus five, plus three times minus twenty.
That is four plus five minus sixty, giving minus fifty one. Notice the middle minus sign turned a subtraction into an addition.
We will evaluate a three by three purely by Sarrus, and then meet the trap that catches careless students.
Mentally copy the first two columns to the right of this grid, so the diagonals have room to run.
Add the three down-right diagonals: one times three times one, plus two times two times two, plus one times zero times one.
That is three, plus eight, plus zero, giving eleven for the down-right sum.
Now subtract the three down-left diagonals: one times three times two, plus one times two times one, plus two times zero times one.
That is six, plus two, plus zero, giving eight for the down-left sum.
The determinant is down-right minus down-left: eleven minus eight, which is three.
<whisper>The exam trap:</whisper> Sarrus works here only because it is three by three. Try this diagonal trick on a four by four and it gives pure nonsense.
We need all values of x for which this symmetric determinant equals zero. Do not expand blindly, exploit the symmetry.
Look at the columns: every column adds up to x plus two. That is the door in.
So do column one becomes column one plus column two plus column three. The first column turns into all x plus two.
Since the whole first column shares the factor x plus two, we pull it straight out of the determinant.
Now clean up: row two becomes row two minus row one, and row three becomes row three minus row one.
That leaves a triangular form with diagonal one, x minus one, x minus one. Its value is x plus two, times x minus one squared.
Set that product to zero. The roots are x equals minus two, or x equals one as a repeated root.
Keep this determinant in mind. It is exactly the one behind the famous k x plus y plus z system we will meet in the inverse part.

Wo ek number random nahi hai. Ye grid ka essence capture karta hai, khaaskar ye ki rows genuinely independent directions mein point kar rahi hain ya nahi.

Three by three grid par jaaiye to determinant us box ka signed volume ban jaata hai jo iski teen rows banaati hain.
Yahaan punchline hai: agar wo volume zero hai, to rows chupke se ek doosre par collapse kar gayi hain aur koi new information nahi rakhtin.

Ek analogy: jaise net run rate poore cricket season ko ek number mein samet deta hai jo team ke baare mein kuchh real batata hai, waise hi determinant poore square table ko ek number mein samet deta hai, jo batata hai ki related system ka ek clean unique answer hai ya nahi.
Value teen tareeqon se likhi jaati hai: d e t A, A ke around vertical bars, ya Greek letter delta. Teenon padhna seekh lijiye.
Bar notation Arthur Cayley ne eighteen forty one mein di, jo Cramer ke seventeen fifty ke equations wale kaam se nikli. Order n determinant mein n factorial terms chhupe hote hain.
Kuchh bhi compute karne se pehle, do non-negotiable rules decide karte hain ki determinant kab banta bhi hai.
Rule one: determinant sirf square matrix ke liye exist karta hai. Ek two by three arrangement ka koi determinant hota hi nahi.
Order one determinant bas entry khud hi hota hai. Yahaan single bar ka matlab determinant hai, modulus nahi.
To determinant of minus five hota hai minus five, chahe uski absolute value five ho. Ye galti lagbhag har koi ek baar karta hai.
Rule two: Sarrus wala diagonal shortcut jo hum aage dekhenge, sirf three by three grids ke liye chalta hai. Ise kabhi two by two ya four by four par mat kheecho.
Iski wajah structural hai. Expansion har row ko ek matching column ke saath pair karta hai, aur sirf square us pairing ko balanced rakhta hai.
Ek aur framing: determinant ek scalar hai, ek pure dimensionless number. Entries ka matlab kuchh bhi ho, iska koi unit nahi hota.
In guardrails ke saath, ab hum aaram se asli expansion machinery bana sakte hain.
Cofactor expansion ki ek reliable four-step rhythm hai. Ise follow karo aur aap shaayad hi sign errors karoge.
Step one, kuchh likhne se pehle, wo row ya column dhoondho jismein sabse zyada zeros hain. Har zero entry ek poora two by two evaluation hata deti hai.
Step two, us chuni hui line ke along chalo. Har entry ke liye, use uske minor se multiply karo, yaani us row aur column ko delete karne ke baad bacha two by two determinant.
Step three, har term par checkerboard sign lagao, minus one to the i plus j.
Step four, saare signed terms ko jod do. Wo sum hi aapka determinant hai.
Signs alternate kyun hote hain? Wo us orientation flip ko encode karte hain jo har baar ek row aur column ke upar se skip karne par hota hai.
Sarrus dense grid par fast hai lekin purely mechanical. Ismein zero-skipping nahi hota, to sparse grid par row expansion jeet jaata hai.
Jab ek unknown x wala determinant kisi value ke barabar rakha jaata hai, to use poora x ke polynomial mein expand karo, phir solve karo. Jab bhi ho sake, pehle simplify karo.
Chaliye ek two by two aur ek three by three evaluate karte hain, har sign ko dhyaan se dekhte hue.
Pehle two by two. Cross-difference: three into four, minus, minus two into five.
Ye hua twelve plus ten, jo deta hai twenty two. Double negative chupke se plus mein badal gaya, iska dhyaan rakho.
Ab three by three. Hum first row ke along expand karenge, plus, minus, plus signs rakhte hue.
Har entry apne minor ke saath pair hoti hai: two into uska minor, minus one into uska minor, plus three into uska minor.
Minors nikalte hain: four minus two is two; zero minus five is minus five; zero minus twenty is minus twenty.
Sab jodne par: two into two, minus one into minus five, plus three into minus twenty.
Ye hua four plus five minus sixty, jo deta hai minus fifty one. Dekho middle minus sign ne subtraction ko addition bana diya.
Hum ek three by three ko purely Sarrus se evaluate karenge, phir wo trap dekhenge jo careless students ko phasata hai.
Is grid ke right mein pehli do columns ko mentally copy karo, taaki diagonals ko chalne ki jagah mile.
Pehle teen down-right diagonals add karo: one into three into one, plus two into two into two, plus one into zero into one.
Ye hua three, plus eight, plus zero, jo down-right sum ke liye eleven deta hai.
Ab teen down-left diagonals subtract karo: one into three into two, plus one into two into one, plus two into zero into one.
Ye hua six, plus two, plus zero, jo down-left sum ke liye eight deta hai.
Determinant hai down-right minus down-left: eleven minus eight, yaani three.
Exam trap ye hai: Sarrus yahaan sirf isliye chalta hai kyunki ye three by three hai. Is diagonal trick ko four by four par lagaoge to pura nonsense aayega.
Humein wo saare x chahiye jinke liye ye symmetric determinant zero hota hai. Blindly expand mat karo, symmetry ka fayda uthao.
Columns dekho: har column ka sum x plus two hai. Yahi andar jaane ka darwaaza hai.
To karo column one becomes column one plus column two plus column three. Pehli column poori x plus two ban jaati hai.
Kyunki poori pehli column mein factor x plus two common hai, hum use determinant se seedha bahar nikaal lete hain.
Ab saaf karo: row two becomes row two minus row one, aur row three becomes row three minus row one.
Ye ek triangular form deta hai jiska diagonal hai one, x minus one, x minus one. Iski value hai x plus two, into x minus one squared.
Us product ko zero rakho. Roots hain x equals minus two, ya x equals one ek repeated root ke roop mein.
Is determinant ko yaad rakho. Ye theek wahi hai jo famous k x plus y plus z system ke peeche hai, jo hum inverse part mein dekhenge.

We want to prove this determinant is zero, without any expansion at all.

Each entry becomes a minus b, plus b minus c, plus c minus a. Everything cancels cleanly to zero.
So the entire first column is now zeros, top to bottom.
A determinant with a full column of zeros is zero by P seven. So delta is zero, and we never expanded.

The takeaway: when rows are built from the same pieces, hunt for a combination that collapses one whole line to zero.
Before touching this determinant, just look at the first two rows and ask if they are related.
Row one is two, four, six. Row two is one, two, three. Do you see it?

Recall from the properties part that a two by two determinant is the signed area of a parallelogram. A triangle is exactly half a parallelogram, so determinants are the natural tool for triangle area from coordinates.

That single fact turns the determinant into a collinearity detector, and pushed one step further, into the equation of the line through two points.

segments.text: Two things deserve a proof: why the formula gives area, and why that third column of ones cannot be dropped.
By the shoelace idea, the signed area of the triangle is one half of the bracket: x one y two minus x two y one, plus x two y three minus x three y two, plus x three y one minus x one y three.
That is the shoelace sum, one half of three paired cross products around the triangle.
Now expand the coordinate determinant along its third column, the column of ones. Each one multiplies the two by two of the other two rows, with the checkerboard signs.
That gives x two y three minus x three y two, minus the bracket x one y three minus x three y one, plus x one y two minus x two y one.

That expansion is exactly twice the shoelace sum, so the geometric area is one half the modulus of delta. And the column of ones is what injects the actual positions of the points, not merely their differences.
The routine: coordinates in the first two columns, ones in the third, expand along that third column, then take one half the modulus for area, or set delta to zero for collinearity.
For a line, replace one vertex by a variable point x, y and demand that delta equals zero. Expanding gives the familiar point-slope line through the two fixed points.
Find the area of the triangle with vertices one two, three five, and minus two four.
Write the coordinates in the first two columns and ones in the third, then expand along the first row.
The three minors are five minus four is one, three minus minus two is five, and twelve minus minus ten is twenty two.
So delta is one, minus ten, plus twenty two, which is thirteen.

segments.text: <curious>Picture a three by three scoreboard, three teams down the side, three stats across.</curious> To weigh one cell, cover its whole row and its whole column, and look only at the smaller grid that survives.
What is left of a three by three is a tidy two by two. The determinant of that surviving grid is the minor of the entry you covered, written M with its row and column subscripts.
So the minor of the row two, column three entry is the determinant of the four cells that survive after you hide that row and that column.
Every entry has its own minor. For a three by three each minor is a two by two determinant; for a four by four, each minor is a three by three.
A cofactor is just a minor with a sign stuck on it. The sign follows a checkerboard, exactly like the light and dark squares of a carrom or chess board.
Position i, j sits on a plus square when i plus j is even, and a minus square when it is odd. Formally the sign is minus one to the power i plus j.
In symbols, C i j equals minus one to the i plus j, times the minor M i j.
Why bake in the sign? Because expansion terms naturally alternate. Folding that alternation into the minor lets us write one clean, sign free rule for the whole determinant.
Beyond the definition, a cofactor has a deeper meaning and hands you two facts that settle most cofactor questions.
A cofactor answers: if I nudge this one entry up a little, how much does the whole determinant change? The cofactor is exactly that sensitivity.
Precisely, the partial derivative of delta with respect to the entry a i j is its cofactor. So small entries paired with large cofactors can still build a big determinant.
Fact one: expand along any row or any column and you get the same determinant. So always choose the line carrying the most zeros, since each zero kills a whole cofactor term.
That is Laplace expansion: delta is the sum along a line of each entry times its own cofactor.
Fact two: pair one row's entries with a different row's cofactors and the sum is exactly zero. Intuitively you would be computing a determinant with one row secretly duplicated.
So the sum of a i j times C k j, taken along the row, is zero whenever i and k differ.
Scope notes: minors and cofactors need a square matrix, the indices start at one, and for a one by one there is nothing left to cover.
Two theorems make this subtopic rigorous, and both reuse a property you already know.

Theorem A says the cross cofactor sum is zero. The proof is slick: build a new matrix by copying row i on top of row k, which does not change row k's cofactors, since those are computed by deleting row k.
Expanding this new matrix along its replaced row gives exactly the cross sum. But the new matrix has two identical rows, so its determinant is zero by the identical rows property.
Combining both facts compactly: the sum is delta when i equals k, and zero otherwise, written with the Kronecker delta.
Theorem B is the power cofactor formula. Start from the adjoint relation, A times adjoint A equals delta times the identity, which is proved in the inverse part.
Take determinants of both sides. Using multiplicativity, and that scaling the identity by delta gives delta to the n, dividing by delta leaves the modulus of the adjoint as delta to the n minus one.
Since the adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix, and transpose does not change a determinant, the cofactor matrix has the same value, delta to the n minus one.
The working routine: strike out the row and column, read the surviving two by two, compute its minor, stamp the checkerboard sign, and for the whole determinant expand along the zero richest line.
Here is every formula this subtopic depends on, gathered in one place.
The minor M i j is the determinant left after deleting row i and column j.
The cofactor is that minor times minus one to the i plus j. Note that the N C E R T textbook writes the same object as A i j.
Laplace expansion works along any row i or any column j: delta is the sum of entries times their own cofactors.
Cross orthogonality, compactly: the sum is delta when the two rows match, and zero when they differ.
The power cofactor formula: the cofactor matrix and the adjoint both have determinant delta to the n minus one; for three by three that is delta squared.
Iterate it and the double adjoint gives delta to the n minus one squared, which for three by three is delta to the fourth.
And the sensitivity identity: the derivative of delta with respect to an entry is that entry's cofactor.
For the given three by three matrix, find the cofactors of the second row entries, then get the determinant by expanding along that row.
Here is the matrix. We will strike out row two each time to build its three cofactors.
Delete row two, column one: the survivor is five minus two, three. Its sign is minus one cubed, so C two one is minus three.
Delete row two, column two: fifteen minus eight is seven, with a plus sign, so C two two is seven.
Delete row two, column three: three minus four is minus one, and the minus sign flips it, so C two three is one.
Expanding along row two: zero times its cofactor, plus two times seven, plus minus one times one, giving fourteen minus one, thirteen.

The whole game is recognising same row versus different row. Same row rebuilds the determinant; a different row secretly duplicates a row and collapses to zero.
So a scary looking pair of sums becomes one short expansion and one instant zero.
Let A be three by three with determinant two. Let C be its cofactor matrix and B the adjoint of the adjoint of A. Find the moduli of C and B.
The cofactor matrix equals the adjoint up to transpose, so its determinant is delta to the n minus one, that is two squared, four.
For B, apply the power formula twice. First the inner adjoint has determinant delta squared, which is four.
Then treat that as the input: its adjoint's determinant is four squared, which is delta to the fourth, sixteen.
The general pattern worth memorising: the double adjoint gives delta to the n minus one squared, which for three by three is delta to the fourth.
The one liner: each adjoint drops the power by one from n, so track n, then n minus one, then n minus one squared.
The classic slip is writing delta to the n instead of delta to the n minus one. For three by three the powers are three, two, and four, not three, three.
These four cofactor mistakes are common in exams. Two one liners let you skip the algebra on most of them.
Pitfall one: reporting the minor as the cofactor. Forgetting the minus one to the i plus j sign is the number one error. Always finish by stamping the sign.
Pitfall two: cross cofactor confusion. Pairing a row's entries with a different row's cofactors gives zero, not the determinant. Same row gives delta, different row gives zero.
Pitfall three: the wrong power in the adjoint. It is delta to the n minus one, not delta to the n. For three by three that is delta squared, not delta cubed.
Pitfall four: expanding along a dense line. Choosing a row or column with no zeros wastes time and multiplies error chances.

<curious>The inverse of a matrix and solving a system turn out to be the same coin.</curious> Start with the inverse.

A matrix A takes a vector and transforms it, stretching, rotating, shearing. The inverse A to the minus one is simply the operation that undoes that transformation, bringing you back to where you started.
Think of a money changer at the airport. Converting rupees to dollars is multiplying by an exchange matrix; converting back is the inverse.
The catch: you can only undo a transformation that did not destroy information. Recall that the determinant is the signed volume of the box spanned by the rows.

If the determinant is zero, the transformation has squashed space flat, a box collapsed onto a plane or a line. Once flattened, infinitely many starting points map to the same place, so there is no unique way back.
That is exactly why a matrix has an inverse if and only if its determinant is nonzero. Such a matrix is called non-singular; a zero determinant makes it singular.
So the whole vocabulary is simple: non-singular means invertible means determinant nonzero, and singular means no inverse means determinant zero.

segments.text: The second face: a linear system in three unknowns is three planes in space, and a solution is a point lying on all three.
When the planes are tilted independently enough, they meet at a single spot, one unique solution, and this is exactly the case when delta is nonzero.
If the planes hinge along a common line, or two or three coincide, they share a whole line or plane, giving infinitely many solutions.
If at least two planes are parallel and offset, like railway tracks that never meet, there is no common point, and the system has no solution. We call it inconsistent.

Delta nonzero is the fingerprint of one unique crossing point. The moment delta is zero, the planes have lost that independence, and you tip into either the infinite or the no-solution world. The right hand side decides which.
For a homogeneous system, all constants zero, every plane passes through the origin, so the trivial solution, all variables zero, always works.
The interesting question is whether they share more than just the origin, a whole line or plane. They do exactly when delta is zero.

One honest caveat: an inverse needs a square non-singular matrix, Cramer's rule is valid only when delta is nonzero, and all the side determinants being zero does not rigorously guarantee infinite solutions. It is a reliable exam rule, not a theorem.
Here is every formula for inverses and systems in one place.
The inverse is one over delta times the adjoint, and the adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.
The fundamental adjoint relation gives delta times the identity, and the determinant of the inverse is one over delta.
The matrix method solves A X equals B as X equals A inverse B, valid only when delta is nonzero.
Cramer's rule: each variable is its own side determinant over delta, where delta i replaces the i-th column with the constants. Valid only when delta is nonzero.

The consistency criterion for a non-homogeneous system: delta nonzero gives unique, delta zero with some side determinant nonzero gives no solution, and delta zero with all side determinants zero gives infinitely many.
For a homogeneous system, the trivial solution always exists, and a non-trivial solution exists exactly when delta is zero.
The one line to carry: no determinant, no inverse. A zero determinant is the whole obstruction.
Solve x plus y plus z equals six, x minus y plus z equals two, and two x plus y minus z equals one.
Write the coefficient matrix A and the constants B.
First delta: one times one minus one, minus one times minus one minus two, plus one times one plus two, which is zero plus three plus three, six. Nonzero, so a unique solution exists.
Compute the nine cofactors and transpose to get the adjoint, shown here.
Then X is one over six times the adjoint times B, which gives one over six times the vector six, twelve, eighteen.
Dividing gives x equals one, y equals two, z equals three.
Check all three: one plus two plus three is six, one minus two plus three is two, two plus two minus three is one. All satisfied.
Classify: x plus two y plus three z equals four, two x plus four y plus six z equals nine, x minus y plus z equals two.
Before computing anything, look at the first two equations. The left side of the second is exactly twice the left side of the first.
So the second left side equals two times the first left side.
So the left sides demand a right side of two times four, eight, but the second equation says nine. A contradiction, so the system is inconsistent, no solution, in one glance.
Setting up Cramer and grinding delta and all three side determinants would waste two minutes to reach the same no solution.
The habit: scan for proportional coefficient rows. If the constants do not match the ratio, the system is inconsistent immediately.
Had the second right side been eight instead of nine, the first two equations would be the same plane, tipping toward infinitely many rather than none.
For k x plus y plus z equals one, x plus k y plus z equals one, x plus y plus k z equals one, find when the system is unique, has no solution, or has infinitely many.
Compute the coefficient determinant as a polynomial in k: it is k cubed minus three k plus two.
Factor it: delta is k minus one squared, times k plus two.
Delta is nonzero when k is neither one nor minus two, so for all other k there is a unique solution.
At k equals one, all three equations collapse to x plus y plus z equals one, the same plane thrice, so infinitely many solutions.
At k equals minus two, adding all three equations gives zero equals three, a contradiction, so no solution.
The template: factor delta as a polynomial in the parameter, then test each root separately for no solution versus infinite. Never assume which one.

segments.text: Here is your complete toolkit for turning a grid into a number. Three formulas, one sign rule.
Order two is the cross-difference: a one one times a two two, minus a one two times a two one.
Order three expands along the first row. Each top entry multiplies the small two by two left after deleting its own row and column.
Burn this in: the middle term carries a minus sign. Forgetting it is the single most common three by three mistake.
The signs follow a checkerboard: plus, minus, plus across the top, then alternating. Formally each term carries minus one to the power i plus j.
You may expand along any row or any column with these signs, and the answer never changes. So pick the line carrying the most zeros.
Sarrus, for three by three only: rewrite the first two columns to the right, add the three down-right diagonals, subtract the three down-left diagonals.
Visually, the down-right diagonals are your plus terms and the down-left diagonals are your minus terms.
One scaling fact to keep you honest: an order n determinant fully expands into n factorial terms. Two for order two, six for order three.
Here is the complete toolkit for this subtopic: one area formula, one collinearity test, one line equation.
Area equals one half the modulus of the determinant whose first two columns hold the coordinates and whose third column is all ones.
Expanded, that is one half the modulus of x one times y two minus y three, plus x two times y three minus y one, plus x three times y one minus y two.
Do not forget either piece. The bare determinant is twice the signed area, so an actual area needs both the one half and the modulus.
The three points are collinear exactly when that same determinant equals zero.
And the line through two points is the set of points x, y making this determinant, with x and y in the first row, equal to zero.
The line determinant simply says a general point x, y lies on the line exactly when it is collinear with the two given points.
All of these are pure numbers. Area comes out in the square units of the coordinate system, with no dimensional formula attached.
Two theorems justify everything: the adjoint relation gives the inverse, and it gives Cramer's rule for free.
Theorem A claims A times the adjoint of A equals delta times the identity. Its i, k entry is the sum of a i j times the adjoint's j, k entry, which is a i j times C k j.
By the cross orthogonality identity from the cofactor part, that sum is delta when i equals k and zero otherwise. So every diagonal entry is delta and every off-diagonal entry is zero.
The corollary is the whole point: if delta is nonzero, divide both sides by delta and A times one over delta times the adjoint equals the identity, so that expression is the inverse.
Theorem B: from X equals A inverse B, the first component is one over delta times the sum of C i one times b i. That sum is the cofactor expansion of delta with its first column replaced by B.
That replaced determinant is exactly delta one, so x equals delta one over delta, and similarly for y and z. That is Cramer's rule.
